result:
I keep returning, in idle moments, to the strangeness of middles. Beginnings get all the philosophical attention—first causes, origins, the spark that starts things—and endings get the rest, since we're creatures obsessed with mortality and conclusion. But middles are where everything actually happens, and almost nobody wants to talk about them. A story's middle is the part writing teachers struggle to explain how to fix. A life's middle is the part nobody throws a party for. You get one for being born and, with luck, a smaller gathering for surviving another year, but the actual texture of the middle—Tuesday afternoon, the dishes, the long stretch between caring deeply about something and finally finishing it—that goes uncelebrated.

I think this is because middles resist narrative. A beginning has the virtue of contrast: there was nothing, now there is something. An ending has the virtue of finality: it lets you look back and assign meaning retroactively, the way you can only see the shape of a wave once it's broken. But the middle is just continuation, and continuation doesn't make for a good story because nothing is being resolved. It's the part where you're still inside the problem, not yet far enough away to describe it.

And yet if I'm honest, almost everything worth doing is mostly middle. Learning an instrument is 2% the thrill of picking it up and 2% the satisfaction of playing something beautiful, and 96% the unglamorous repetition in between, where your fingers don't do what you want and you can't tell if you're improving. Relationships are like this too—the falling in love and the dramatic reconciliations or breakups are brief, vivid, narratable; the rest is just two people in a kitchen, negotiating who does the dishes, building something neither of them can quite see while they're inside it. Most of what we call "a life" is this kind of middle, and it's strange that we have so few cultural tools for appreciating it on its own terms, rather than treating it as mere transit between more meaningful points.

I wonder if part of the reason is that middles require a different kind of attention than beginnings or endings do. A beginning asks you to notice change—here is the new thing, distinct from what came before. An ending asks you to notice completion—here is the shape now that it's whole. But a middle asks you to notice without the aid of contrast or closure. You have to find interest in something that isn't differentiating itself from anything, that isn't moving toward a visible resolution. This is much harder. It's the difference between admiring a sunset, which announces its own beauty through dramatic change, and admiring an ordinary Tuesday sky, which does nothing to earn your attention and yet, if you actually look at it, is doing the same quiet work of being a sky that the sunset is.

Meditation traditions seem to understand this better than most. A lot of contemplative practice is just training yourself to notice middles—the unremarkable present moment, neither beginning nor ending, which turns out to be the only moment you ever actually have. The whole conceit of a narrative life, where things are building toward something or resolving from something, is revealed under quiet attention to be a kind of story we tell ourselves about time, laid over a present that doesn't actually care about narrative structure at all. The present moment has no plot. It just is, the way the middle of a song is still music even though it isn't the hook.

I notice this same blindness toward middles in how people think about effort and skill. We lionize the eureka moment and the finished masterpiece, but the actual development of any skill is a long middle of plateau, where you can't tell if you're getting better, where the feedback is sparse and ambiguous, where most of your effort produces no visible result. People drop out of things during the middle far more often than at the beginning or end, because the middle offers the least reinforcement. It's the section of any project where faith matters most, because evidence is thinnest. I suspect a huge amount of human potential is lost not at the hard parts, exactly, but at the boring parts—the ones that don't even have the dignity of being hard, just long.

Maybe what middles need is not more drama but a different standard of value entirely—not "is this leading somewhere" but "is this, in itself, alive." A conversation's middle, once the pleasantries are done and before the goodbyes start, is often the only part that was ever really a conversation, the only part where two minds were actually doing something together rather than performing the rituals that bookend doing something together. If you measure a conversation only by its opening charm and its closing warmth, you miss the entire conversation.

I don't know if this adds up to advice, exactly. Maybe it's just an observation: that we have built our entire emotional vocabulary around contrast and closure, and as a result we are somewhat impoverished when it comes to perceiving duration, continuity, the textured present that doesn't resolve into anything. The middle is not a problem to be solved or a delay before the good part. It might, in fact, be most of what there is. The trick—and I don't claim to have it—would be learning to want to be there, in the middle, without needing it to be going anywhere, the way you might enjoy being in a room with someone without needing the conversation to lead to a conclusion. Just two people, in the middle of something, which is also, it turns out, the middle of everything.
